Chapter 3: Aligning Spending with Values and True Needs
Now that you’ve got a clear picture of where your money’s going, it’s time to ask—are those dollars actually supporting what matters most to you?
This next step is all about realignment. It’s about moving away from automatic habits, and making choices that honestly reflect your own values and real needs.
Think about the world we live in. Everywhere you look—ads, social media, even conversations with friends—there’s this constant push to spend, as if buying more is the secret to happiness, status, or belonging.
But here’s something to pay attention to: Once your basic needs are met, research shows that more stuff doesn’t bring lasting satisfaction. Sure, that new gadget or outfit might give you a quick thrill, but it fades fast. What sticks around is the deeper desire for meaning and connection.
So, how do you break out of that cycle? Start by looking at the difference between wants and needs. Needs are those essentials—like food, a safe place to live, your health, and a sense of security. Wants? They’re the extras, and they’re often shaped by what’s going on around you.
This isn’t about denying yourself pleasure. It’s simply about making choices with your eyes open.
Here’s a simple exercise you can try: Go through your recent spending and ask yourself a few honest questions. Did this purchase really meet a need, or was I just acting out of habit or emotion?
How much satisfaction did it actually bring me—right away, and even days later? And, if I had the chance to choose again, would I spend my money the same way?
You might be surprised by what you find. Maybe you’ve got a gym membership that barely gets used, while a small splurge on art supplies gives you hours of genuine joy. Or, maybe those takeout meals happen more often when you’re stressed, not because you actually love them.
Aligning your spending with your values means figuring out what’s most important to you—like close relationships, creativity, your health, learning something new, or making a difference. Then, it’s about steering your money toward those things. Sometimes, that means cutting back on purchases made just for status, and investing more in experiences or activities that really help you grow or connect.
Want some practical steps? Try this:
First, categorize each expense by how much lasting satisfaction it brings—high, medium, or low.
Next, take a moment to reflect on your core values. What actually fills your life with meaning, regardless of what others might expect?
And finally, start adjusting your spending—little by little—so it lines up with your priorities.
Remember, this isn’t a one-and-done deal. As your life changes, so will your values and your financial choices. The aim isn’t to be perfect—it’s about making progress. Moving closer to a life where your money genuinely supports your well-being, instead of being the end goal.
When you let your spending reflect your values, something amazing happens. You discover you can enjoy more satisfaction with less. You start to challenge that old belief that more is always better. And, you open the door to a simpler, more intentional way of living.
